cmocs.statement: In undergraduate medical students, repeated computer-based patient cases augmented with formative key feature questions and detailed feedback supported learning from errors/successes and improved later performance compared with repeated case-based study alone.
cmocs.supporting_quote: Detailed feedback was created for each item; students were able to access this feedback by clicking on a specific button... 33.3% of students who failed to provide a correct answer in one test went on to submit a correct answer in a subsequent test of the same item, thus suggesting a learning effect elicited by the feedback provided.

cmocs.statement: Among undergraduate medical students, repeated testing embedded in case-based e-seminars produced higher long-term retention test scores than repeated study of the same cases without questions.
cmocs.supporting_quote: In the retention test, mean student scores on intervention items were significantly higher than those on control items (56.0 ± 25.8% versus 48.8 ± 24.7%; p < 0.001)... repeated testing was more effective than repeated case-based learning alone.

cmocs.statement: Using longitudinal key feature testing with authentic patient cases had a positive impact on learning outcomes in relevant aspects of clinical medicine for undergraduate students.
cmocs.supporting_quote: This is the first study to demonstrate an effect of test-enhanced learning on clinical reasoning as assessed with key feature questions... Curricular implementation of longitudinal key feature testing may considerably enhance student learning outcomes in relevant aspects of clinical medicine.

coder_notes: Paper clearly concerns undergraduate medical students (E01). The intervention is repeated testing within computer-based patient cases; the closest available intervention code is strategies that promote knowledge retention (E12), with real-life/patient case scenarios (E10). Detailed feedback is explicitly described and linked to improvement (E13 -> E42). Outcomes are improved learning/performance/retention, best captured by E46, with broader positive learning impact (E28/E40) where stated. The paper discusses intuitive and analytic reasoning in the introduction, but the intervention did not explicitly instruct students to use analytical reasoning alone or dual-process reasoning, so E08/E18 were not coded. No defensible evidence for mechanisms such as understanding (E20), cognitive load, frustration, fear, or illness scripts.
